topic.en: Three sections: village hall hire and a riverbank clean-up, the probation period and company vehicles, and an essay on why every map distorts.
topic.kk: Үш бөлім: ауыл залын жалдау мен жағалауды тазалау, сынақ мерзімі мен қызметтік көлік, кез келген картаның неге бұрмалайтыны туралы очерк.
topic.ru: Три секции: аренда сельского зала и уборка берега, испытательный срок и служебные машины, очерк о том, почему любая карта искажает.

paragraphs.text: Ashcombe Village Hall — hire information. The main hall holds one hundred and twenty people seated, or eighty with tables, and the small room at the back holds twenty. Hire is £14 an hour for the main hall and £8 for the small room, with a minimum of two hours; local groups that meet weekly pay a reduced rate of £9 and £5. A deposit of £50 is taken for parties and returned within a week if the hall is left as it was found.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: The kitchen is included with the main hall and has an oven, a large fridge and a water heater, but no dishwasher; crockery for a hundred is in the cupboards and is counted after each booking. Alcohol may be served at a private party without a licence but may not be sold; if you intend to sell it, you must apply to the council at least ten working days in advance and show us the licence before the event.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: Bookings are made through the caretaker, by telephone in the evening or on the form in the porch. Music must stop at 11 pm and everybody must be out by midnight, as the hall stands next to houses; the caretaker locks up and will not wait beyond that. Bins hold ordinary rubbish only and there is no recycling collection at the hall, so bottles and cans go home with you. Tables and chairs are stacked in the store at the end, in the order shown on the photograph by the door.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: Riverbank clean-up day — information for volunteers. We meet at the old mill car park at 9.30 am on the last Saturday of the month, from March to November. Sessions last about three hours, and you may leave earlier if you tell a team leader. Anybody over fourteen may take part; those under sixteen need a parent to sign the form on arrival, and children under fourteen may come along but may not work at the water’s edge.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: We provide gloves, litter pickers, bags and high-visibility vests; bring boots and a waterproof, as the work goes ahead in rain and is cancelled only when the river is high. Do not bring waders: nobody enters the water. Sharp items, anything in a sealed container and anything you cannot identify are left where they are and reported to a team leader, who has the equipment to deal with them.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: The bags are collected from the car park by the council on the Monday, so please stack them there rather than beside the path. We record the weight and the kinds of rubbish found, and the record goes to the river trust, which uses it to argue for better bins upstream; this is the part of the day that changes anything, so the recording sheet matters as much as the picking. Tea and cake are provided at the end by the shop at the bridge, which asks only that you take your mug back to the counter.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: Your probation period: what to expect. New employees serve six months, during which either side may end the contract with one week’s notice rather than the month that applies afterwards. The period exists to check that the job and the person fit each other, and the company treats it as a two-way test: you are also deciding whether to stay, and the review asks you as well as your manager.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: There are three formal conversations, at six weeks, three months and five months, and they are booked when you join rather than arranged when somebody remembers. Each is written up on one page, signed by both, and kept; nothing that appears in a final review should be a surprise at that point, and a manager who raises a problem for the first time at five months has failed the process rather than the employee.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: Training during probation is not optional and is paid: the induction week, the safety course for your area, and two half-days with another team so that you see where your work goes. If a piece of training has not happened by the three-month conversation, that is recorded as an action for the manager. Holiday accrues from the first day and may be taken during probation with the usual notice, though not in the first month.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: Probation may be extended once, by up to three months, where a specific difficulty has been identified and a plan agreed; it is not extended simply because a manager is undecided. If the period ends without a decision being communicated, employment continues on the ordinary terms, and the company treats that as its own error rather than the employee’s risk. Where probation is not passed, the reason is given in writing and the employee may reply in writing, which is kept with the file.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: Using company vehicles. Before driving any vehicle for the first time you show your licence to the transport office, which checks it against the driving record held by the authority and repeats that check every six months. You must report points, a disqualification or a medical condition affecting driving on the day you learn of it; the report is to the transport office and not to your line manager, and it is treated as a licensing matter rather than a disciplinary one.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: A vehicle is checked before each shift using the card in the cab: lights, tyres, fluid levels, mirrors, load security and the warning lights on the dashboard. A defect that affects safety takes the vehicle off the road immediately and is reported by telephone; a defect that does not is written on the card and dealt with at the next service. Driving a vehicle with a reported safety defect is treated as seriously as driving without a licence.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: Fuel is bought with the vehicle card at the stations listed in the cab, and the receipt goes into the wallet with the mileage written on the back. Personal use of a company vehicle is not permitted except for the journey home when a shift ends away from the depot, which is agreed in advance. Passengers who are not employees may not be carried, including family members, and this rule has no exceptions for short distances.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: After an incident, however small, stop, make the scene safe and telephone the transport office before moving the vehicle unless it is blocking traffic. Exchange details with the other driver, photograph the position of the vehicles, and do not discuss fault with anybody at the scene; the company’s insurer decides that and a statement made at the roadside is worth more to the other side than to us. A damaged vehicle returns to the depot only if it is safe to drive, and that judgement is made by the transport office rather than by the driver.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: Every map is wrong, and the useful question is how. A map is a flat picture of a curved surface reduced several hundred thousand times, drawn for a purpose, and each of those three facts forces a distortion that cannot be removed, only moved somewhere less inconvenient. Readers who know this treat a map as an argument; readers who do not treat it as a photograph, and a photograph is exactly what a map is not.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: The curvature problem is the famous one. A sphere cannot be flattened without stretching, so a projection must choose what to preserve: shape, area, distance or direction, and never all of them at once. The projection that keeps a compass bearing as a straight line, which is why it was drawn and why ships used it for centuries, enlarges everything far from the equator; the projections that keep areas honest bend the shapes instead. Neither is a lie, and both are described as one by people who have only met the other.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: Scale forces a second set of choices that mapmakers call generalisation. A coastline drawn at one scale has bays that vanish at another, a village becomes a dot, two roads that run a few metres apart become one line, and a river is smoothed until it stops meandering. The rules for doing this well are old and are mostly about what to keep rather than what to remove: a small lake beside a road is kept because travellers use it to know where they are, while a larger one in empty country may be dropped.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: Purpose is the third and is the least discussed. A map for walkers shows paths, contours and field boundaries and leaves out the bus routes; a map for drivers shows junctions and omits the footbridge that joins two halves of a village; a map made for a utility shows its own pipes in detail and everything else as background. Each is accurate and each is silent about most of the world, and a reader who takes one to answer a question it was not drawn for will be misled by a map that is not wrong.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: Digital maps have changed which distortions matter. Zooming in and out means a reader meets several generalisations in a minute without noticing the transitions, and the same place can appear to have a road that disappears at the next zoom level. Labels are placed by software that must decide, in a fraction of a second, which of two names to omit when they overlap, and that decision is invisible to the reader and consistent in ways that a hand-drawn map never was.
paragraphs.label: E

paragraphs.text: What is on a map is also a political statement, and mapmakers have long been careful about it. Borders that are disputed are drawn differently for different markets, names of places appear in the form preferred by the buyer, and a large mapping service will hold several versions of the same region for this reason. This is not a scandal so much as an unavoidable consequence of selling one product into places that disagree, and the honest response is to say which version a reader is looking at.
paragraphs.label: F

paragraphs.text: The most consequential distortion now is not on the map at all but in what is missing from it. Places that are not mapped in detail are places where services are hard to plan: an informal settlement without street names does not appear in a routing system, and an ambulance sent there arrives late or not at all. Volunteer mapping projects have filled parts of this gap, working from satellite images and local knowledge, and their work is used by emergency services in a way its authors did not foresee.
paragraphs.label: G

paragraphs.text: The practical advice is unglamorous and has not changed in a century. Read the scale, read the legend, notice the date, ask what the map was drawn for, and remember that anything absent may be absent because it is not there or because it was not the point. A map is a compressed argument about a place, made by somebody with a purpose, and it is useful in proportion to how clearly the reader understands that purpose.
paragraphs.label: H
